```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsforecast import StatsForecast
from statsforecast.models import (MSTL, HistoricAverage, Naive,
                                  RandomWalkWithDrift, SeasonalNaive)
from utilsforecast.losses import mae, mape, mase, rmse, rmsse, scaled_crps

from coursekit import datasets as D
from coursekit import plotting as P

P.use_course_style()

spine = D.spine()
H = 24
train, test = D.train_test(spine, h=H)

MODELS = ["HistoricAverage", "Naive", "SeasonalNaive", "RWD", "MSTL"]
LABELS = {"HistoricAverage": "Mean", "Naive": "Naive",
          "SeasonalNaive": "Seasonal naive", "RWD": "Drift",
          "MSTL": "STL + drift"}

# One ladder of levels for every forecast: 80 is what coverage is read off,
# the rest let Ch 5.9 score the whole distribution.
LEVELS = [20, 40, 60, 80, 95]
QCOLS = ["lo-95", "lo-80", "lo-60", "lo-40", "lo-20",
         "hi-20", "hi-40", "hi-60", "hi-80", "hi-95"]
QUANTILES = np.array([0.025, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 0.975])

sf = StatsForecast(
    models=[HistoricAverage(), Naive(), SeasonalNaive(season_length=12),
            RandomWalkWithDrift(),
            MSTL(season_length=12, trend_forecaster=RandomWalkWithDrift())],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)
fc = sf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=LEVELS)
merged = test.merge(fc, on=["unique_id", "ds"])

# Rolling-origin cross-validation: 8 origins, one year forecast each.
N_WINDOWS, CV_H = 8, 12
cv = sf.cross_validation(df=spine, h=CV_H, step_size=CV_H,
                         n_windows=N_WINDOWS, level=LEVELS)

per_window = pd.DataFrame([
    mase(g.drop(columns=["cutoff"]), models=MODELS, seasonality=12,
         train_df=spine[spine["ds"] <= cut])[MODELS].iloc[0]
    for cut, g in cv.groupby("cutoff")
]).reset_index(drop=True)

coverage = {m: float(((cv["y"] >= cv[f"{m}-lo-80"])
                      & (cv["y"] <= cv[f"{m}-hi-80"])).mean()) for m in MODELS}
width80 = {m: float((cv[f"{m}-hi-80"] - cv[f"{m}-lo-80"]).mean()) for m in MODELS}
crps = {m: float(scaled_crps(cv.drop(columns=["cutoff"]),
                             models={m: [f"{m}-{c}" for c in QCOLS]},
                             quantiles=QUANTILES)[m].iloc[0]) for m in MODELS}
```

# A. Scoring a point forecast {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 5.8 · Point forecast metrics

## Only a scaled metric can compare across series

Forecast error: $e_{T+h} = y_{T+h} - \hat{y}_{T+h|T}$

| Metric | Property | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **MAE** | Easy to interpret | Scale-dependent: cannot be pooled across series |
| **RMSE** | Punishes large errors | Scale-dependent |
| **MAPE** | Unit-free | Explodes near zero, and asymmetric |
| **MASE** | **Scaled**: MAE over the benchmark's | Needs the seasonal period |
| **RMSSE** | **Scaled**: RMSE over the benchmark's | Same, and still punishes outliers |

::: {.notes}
MAE and RMSE work well within a single series. To compare across different products or series, use MASE.
:::

## Rescaling the data moves MAE but not MASE

Same series, new unit, with $k > 0$: $y'_t = k\,y_t$ and $\hat{y}'_t = k\,\hat{y}_t$.

. . .

$$\text{MAE}' = \frac{1}{n}\sum \lvert k y_t - k\hat{y}_t \rvert = k\,\text{MAE}
\quad\text{(moves with the unit)}$$

. . .

$$PE'_t = \frac{k y_t - k\hat{y}_t}{k y_t} = PE_t
\qquad
\text{MASE}' = \frac{k\,\text{MAE}}{k\,Q} = \text{MASE}$$

. . .

Now shift as well as scale, $y'_t = k y_t + c$, which is what °C to °F is.
Differences kill $c$, so MASE holds. MAPE's denominator keeps it.

::: {.cardbox}
MAPE cancelled $k$ and is still the worst metric in this deck. Cancelling is necessary, not sufficient.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do this one at the board pace, not the slide pace. Ask what happens to each
metric if the finance team reports the same series in thousands instead of
dollars. Everyone knows MAE has to move. Then substitute.

MAE picks up the k and moves with the unit. MAPE cancels it, top and bottom.
MASE cancels it too, and the reason is worth saying out loud: Q is built from
the same data, so the denominator scales by exactly the same k as the numerator.
That cancellation is the licence for what Day 1 did when it pooled 148 retail
series with different turnovers into one ranking.

Then the sting. MAPE passed the test and is still the worst metric in this deck,
so cancelling k is necessary and not sufficient. Add an offset and the two part
company: every term in MASE is a difference, so c disappears, but MAPE divides
by a level and the c rides along. That is the temperature objection, three
slides early, and now it is a consequence rather than an assertion.
:::

## MAPE explodes when the actual is near zero

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
low = D.low_volume_demand(n=48, seed=3)
preds = low[["ds"]].assign(A=low["y"] + 2.0, B=low["y"] - 0.15)

P.forecast_overlay(low, preds, ["A", "B"], colors=[P.ORANGE, P.BLUE],
                   labels={"A": "forecast A (+2.0)", "B": "forecast B (-0.15)"},
                   history_tail=None, history_label="actual (low volume)",
                   figsize=(10, 3.6), title="Low-volume demand breaks MAPE")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: simulated low-volume / intermittent demand (Poisson counts near zero)
low = D.low_volume_demand(n=48, seed=3)
preds = low[["ds"]].assign(A=low["y"] + 2.0,      # always 2 units too high
                           B=low["y"] - 0.15)     # always 0.15 too low

P.forecast_overlay(low, preds, ["A", "B"], history_tail=None,
                   history_label="actual (low volume)")
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- Forecast A: MAE = 2.00, MAPE = **304%**
- Forecast B: MAE = 0.15, MAPE = **23%**
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the two forecasts off the chart before quoting the numbers, and let the
room commit. Forecast A is two units too high everywhere; forecast B is fifteen
hundredths too low everywhere. Everyone picks B, and everyone is right.

Then show the MAPE column: A scores 304%, B scores 23%. MAPE agrees here. Now
ask what happens when the actual is 0.2 and you are two units out - the
percentage error is a thousand percent, and it is the denominator doing that,
not the forecast.
:::

## Three reasons MAPE cannot select a model

::: {.incremental}
1. **Undefined at zero**: explodes on intermittent / low-volume demand
2. **Asymmetric**: penalizes over-forecasting far more than under-forecasting
3. **Fails without a true zero**: the offset never cancels, so °C breaks it
:::

::: {.notes}
The second one surprises people, so make it concrete. Forecast 100 when the
actual is 50 and MAPE charges you 100%. Forecast 50 when the actual is 100 and
it charges you 50%. The same 50-unit error, twice the penalty for being high. A
team that selects on MAPE learns to under-forecast, and in an inventory setting
that means stocking out.

The third is the one people argue with, and the rescaling slide already
answered it. MAPE needs a meaningful zero to divide by, and 0 degrees Celsius is
not "no temperature", it is a point on a scale somebody chose. Convert to
Fahrenheit and the offset survives in the denominator, so the same forecast
scores differently in the two units. MASE, built from differences, does not
care.

None of this makes MAPE useless. It reports well to a business audience. It just
cannot be the thing you select a model on.
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox}
Report MAPE to executives if required, but **never optimize models using MAPE**.
:::

## Dividing by the benchmark makes errors comparable

Error divided by the in-sample Seasonal Naive error ($Q$):

$$\text{MASE} = \frac{\text{MAE}}{Q},
\qquad Q = \frac{1}{T-m}\sum_{t=m+1}^{T} \lvert y_t - y_{t-m} \rvert$$

$Q$ is measured in the units of the data, which is what cancelled the $k$.

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- **$\text{MASE} < 1$** $\rightarrow$ **Better** than the seasonal naive baseline
- **$\text{MASE} = 1$** $\rightarrow$ Exactly as good as seasonal naive
- **$\text{MASE} > 1$** $\rightarrow$ **Worse** than simple baseline
:::

::: {.notes}
The denominator is the whole idea: divide by the in-sample one-step seasonal
naive error, and the metric becomes scale-free and readable. MASE below 1 beats
the benchmark, above 1 loses to it.

Warn them the seasonal naive will score above 1 on this data, and that this is
not a contradiction: forecasting 24 months out is harder than the one-step
in-sample errors sitting in the denominator.
:::

## On this one window the STL route wins every metric

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "MAE": mae(merged, models=MODELS)[MODELS].iloc[0],
    "RMSE": rmse(merged, models=MODELS)[MODELS].iloc[0],
    "MAPE %": mape(merged, models=MODELS)[MODELS].iloc[0] * 100,
    "MASE": mase(merged, models=MODELS, seasonality=12, train_df=train)[MODELS].iloc[0],
    "RMSSE": rmsse(merged, models=MODELS, seasonality=12, train_df=train)[MODELS].iloc[0],
})
scores.index = [LABELS[m] for m in scores.index]
print(scores.round(2).to_string())
```

::: {.cardbox .coral}
On **this window** the STL route wins on every metric ($\text{MASE} = 0.70$), with the
seasonal naive second at $1.11$. Hold that thought until part B.
:::

::: {.notes}
Resist declaring a winner here. The seasonal naive's MASE > 1.0 because forecasting
24 months ahead is harder than the in-sample one-step naive errors in the
denominator. The STL route's 0.70 is the number that gets a model promoted on one
lucky year, and part B of this deck takes it back.

RMSSE is the same idea as MASE with squared errors, which is why the two columns
agree on the ranking here and why both end up on the leaderboard.
:::

# B. One split is not evidence {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 5.10 · Rolling-origin cross-validation

## One split gives a number with no error bar

::: {.incremental}
- A single 24-month split is just **one sample point**
- Score depends heavily on economic conditions during that window
- High variance ($\pm 16\%$ error bars on 24 observations)
- Encourages data snooping and overfitting
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
Time series cannot use standard k-fold. We need **rolling origins**.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the hinge of the day. One split gives one number, and one number has no
error bar, so it cannot support a ranking.

Ask the room how confident they would be in a drug trial with one patient. Same
objection, same fix: more origins.
:::

## Rolling the origin turns one score into a distribution

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
P.cv_staircase(n_obs=144, initial=48, horizon=12, step=12, figsize=(9, 3.9),
               title="Eight origins, one year forecast each")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Diagram: the eight folds this deck scores on, drawn to scale.
# 144 periods, initial train 48, horizon 12, step 12 -> 8 origins.
P.cv_staircase(n_obs=144, initial=48, horizon=12, step=12)
```

:::

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Each fold trains only on past data. **No fold ever peeks into its future**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the diagram fold by fold. Blue is what the model saw, orange is what it was
scored on, grey is the future it was not allowed to know about. Every row moves
the boundary forward and never backwards.

Say explicitly why k-fold is wrong here: shuffling puts future rows in the
training set, which is leakage, and the last slide of this deck comes back to it.
:::

## Three knobs control the CV: h, step_size and n_windows

```python
# Rolling-origin CV on the spine:
cv = sf.cross_validation(
    df=spine,
    h=12,          # Forecast horizon matched to business need
    step_size=12,  # Steps between successive origins
    n_windows=8,   # Number of evaluation folds
    level=[80],
)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **`h`**: match the true operational planning horizon
- **`step_size`**: frequency of forecast production
- **`n_windows`**: number of independent test origins
:::

::: {.notes}
Pick h from the decision, not from the data. If the plan is quarterly, h is
three, and a model that wins at h=12 is not the one you want.

The trade in n_windows is honest: more windows is a steadier estimate and a
shorter first training set. Eight is what this series affords.
:::

## Eight folds keep the ranking and move the winner

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
single = mase(merged, models=MODELS, seasonality=12, train_df=train)[MODELS].iloc[0]
SHOWN = ["Naive", "SeasonalNaive", "RWD", "MSTL"]
P.single_vs_cv_plot(single, per_window[SHOWN], labels=LABELS, ylim=(0, 4.2),
                    figsize=(10, 3.4), ylabel="MASE",
                    note="the mean model is off the top of this axis at 12.25",
                    titles=("Stable ranking, except at the top",
                            "Score distribution across folds"))
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Score EVERY fold separately, each against its own training history: a fold's
# MASE denominator must come from data that fold was allowed to see.
per_window = pd.DataFrame([
    mase(g.drop(columns=["cutoff"]), models=MODELS, seasonality=12,
         train_df=spine[spine["ds"] <= cut])[MODELS].iloc[0]
    for cut, g in cv.groupby("cutoff")
])

single = mase(merged, models=MODELS, seasonality=12, train_df=train)[MODELS].iloc[0]
P.single_vs_cv_plot(single, per_window[MODELS], labels=LABELS)
```

:::

::: {.notes}
Notice the right plot: for Seasonal Naive, individual fold MASE ranges from 0.71 to 1.90. The single split was lucky or unlucky; the 8-fold average is what to trust.
:::
::: {.cardbox .coral}
One window crowned **STL + drift** at 0.70. Eight folds hand it back, 1.18 to 1.22.
:::


## Only the seasonal naive's band is close to honest

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
P.coverage_bars({m: coverage[m] for m in MODELS}, nominal=0.8, labels=LABELS,
                figsize=(9, 3.4),
                title=f"80% interval coverage ({N_WINDOWS * CV_H} scored points)")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian takeaway food turnover (cv across 8 origins x 12 horizon = 96 points)
# Coverage = share of holdout points falling between the 80% lo/hi bounds.
coverage = {m: float(((cv["y"] >= cv[f"{m}-lo-80"])
                      & (cv["y"] <= cv[f"{m}-hi-80"])).mean()) for m in MODELS}

P.coverage_bars(coverage, nominal=0.8, labels=LABELS)
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Seasonal Naive**: 77% coverage (near nominal 80%)
- **Mean Model**: 0% coverage (fails on trending data)
:::

::: {.notes}
The mean model scores exactly 0%. Not "poorly" - zero. On a series that grew
sixfold, an interval centred on the historical average never touches the last
few years at all, and that is worth pausing on: a model can be so wrong that its
uncertainty estimate is not even wrong in an interesting way.

The seasonal naive's 77% against a nominal 80% is the honest result here, and
96% on the single window in lecture 1 is the same interval measured badly.
:::

## Coverage checks the band. It cannot rank.

Ch 5.9 · Scoring the whole distribution

::: {.incremental}
- Coverage answers one question: **is the 80% band honest?**
- It says nothing about **width**: an interval of $\pm\infty$ covers 100%
- Two models at 80% coverage can be worlds apart in usefulness
- A **proper score** charges you for width *and* for misses, in one number
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
**Scaled CRPS** averages the quantile (pinball) loss over the whole ladder of
levels. Scale-free, lower is better, and you can sort on it.
:::

::: {.notes}
The infinity example is the one that lands: an interval of plus or minus
infinity has perfect coverage and zero value. Coverage is a pass/fail check on
honesty, not a score.

That is what a proper score fixes, and it is why LEVELS has five entries rather
than just 80 - scaled CRPS needs a ladder of quantiles to integrate over.
:::

## Narrow is not the same as good

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.width_vs_crps_plot(width80, {m: crps[m] for m in MODELS}, coverage=coverage,
                     labels=LABELS, level=80, figsize=(10, 3.4))
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian takeaway food turnover, 8 rolling origins x 12 months
from utilsforecast.losses import scaled_crps

QCOLS = ["lo-95", "lo-80", "lo-60", "lo-40", "lo-20",
         "hi-20", "hi-40", "hi-60", "hi-80", "hi-95"]
QUANTILES = np.array([0.025, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 0.975])

crps = {m: scaled_crps(cv.drop(columns=["cutoff"]),
                       models={m: [f"{m}-{c}" for c in QCOLS]},
                       quantiles=QUANTILES)[m].iloc[0] for m in MODELS}
```

:::

::: {.cardbox .coral}
The STL route's intervals are the **narrowest** here, and it still loses on CRPS.
Narrowness that is not earned gets charged for.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the Ch 5.9 payoff, so give it the time. It is the slide that stops "my
intervals are tighter" from being an argument.

The STL route has the narrower 80% band - about 40 units against the seasonal
naive's 49 - and it loses on CRPS, 0.034 to 0.031, because those narrow bands
miss more often: 61% coverage against 77%. Tighter is only better if you were
right, and CRPS is what prices that trade in one number.
:::

## Leakage is a model seeing its own future

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 9.5
digraph G {
    bgcolor="transparent";
    rankdir=LR;
    node [shape=box style="rounded,filled" fontsize=12
          color="#1C355E" penwidth=2 margin="0.16,0.09"];
    edge [fontsize=11 color="#5b6678" penwidth=1.6];

    A [label="Scaling or normalising\non the full series" fillcolor="#FF7A5C" fontcolor="white"];
    B [label="Centred rolling\nwindow features" fillcolor="#FF7A5C" fontcolor="white"];
    C [label="Tuning hyperparameters\non the test set" fillcolor="#FF7A5C" fontcolor="white"];
    L [label="Data Leakage\nOver-optimistic CV,\npoor production" fillcolor="#1C355E" fontcolor="white"];

    A -> L; B -> L; C -> L;
}
```

::: {.notes}
Always fit scalers, imputers, and feature engineering strictly on each fold's
training history. The third box is the one that gets past code review, because
nobody wrote a line that looks wrong - they just kept trying models until the
test score improved. The next slide runs that one.
:::

## Choosing per fold with the answer in hand buys 24%

```{python}
#| echo: true
honest = per_window["SeasonalNaive"].mean()      # rule fixed in advance
oracle = per_window[MODELS].min(axis=1).mean()   # best model per fold

print(f"seasonal naive, every fold  : MASE {honest:.2f}")
print(f"best model, chosen per fold : MASE {oracle:.2f}")
print(f"discount bought by peeking  : {1 - oracle / honest:.0%}")
```

::: {.cardbox .coral}
No rule available *before* a fold produces the second number. It is the holdout
leaking into the choice of model.
:::

::: {.notes}
Run this one live. The seasonal naive wins four folds and the STL route wins the
other four, and swapping between them fold by fold takes the average from 1.18
to 0.90 - a 24% improvement bought entirely by knowing the answer first.

Ask the room what rule they would have written in advance to make those swaps.
There isn't one. That is the whole definition of leakage: a number produced by a
decision that could not have been made at forecast time.

This is also the honest version of what happened in lecture 1, where a single
window crowned the STL route at 0.70.
:::

## Four ways an honest team still fools itself

::: {.incremental}
- **Regime changes**: verify if old folds disagree with recent folds
- **Underpowered sample**: evaluate over sufficient origins ($>50$ points)
- **Overlapping folds**: beware overly narrow confidence intervals when `step_size < h`
- **Data gaps**: verify timestamp continuity across all origins
:::

::: {.notes}
None of these require anyone to be careless. Every one of them has shipped from
a competent team.

If you have a war story, this is where it goes. If not, the honest version is
the one this course just walked through: a single window crowned the STL route
at 0.70 and eight windows handed it back.
:::
